```{r}
#| label: setup
source("functions.R")
```

# 1. What population are you sampling from?

This is the fatigue example from the class handout. A player takes n shots in a game. Shot t is made (1) or missed (0)
with probability p_t, and fatigue makes p_t fall evenly from 0.9 on the first shot to 0.5 on the last one. The shots
are independent of each other. The sample mean is the player's shooting percentage for the game.

The CLT assumptions: the shots are independent and every shot has a finite variance, but they are not identically
distributed, because every shot has its own p_t. So this tests the second assumption.

In the handout one game has 20 shots. To study how the shooting percentage behaves as n grows, I let the number of
shots in a game be n and spread the same fatigue (0.9 down to 0.5) over those n shots.

```{r}
#| label: oneGame
#| fig.width: 8
#| fig.height: 4.5
set.seed(student_id)
nShots <- 20
p20 <- shotProbs(nShots)
made <- rbinom(nShots, size = 1, prob = p20)
plot(1:nShots, p20, type = "b", pch = 19, ylim = c(0, 1), col = "firebrick",
     xlab = "Shot number", ylab = "Probability / outcome",
     main = paste0("One game of 20 shots (seed ", student_id, ")"))
points(1:nShots, made, pch = 19, col = "steelblue", cex = 1.2)
legend("bottomleft", c("Probability of a make", "Actual outcome"), col = c("firebrick", "steelblue"),
       lty = c(1, NA), pch = 19, bty = "n")
```

In this game the player made `r sum(made)` of 20 shots, a shooting percentage of `r round(mean(made), 2)`.

## Theory for any n

Because the shots are independent, the mean and variance of the shooting percentage add up shot by shot:

* Mean: the average of the p_t, which is (0.9 + 0.5) / 2 = 0.7 for every n of 2 or more.
* Standard error: sqrt(Σ p_t (1 − p_t)) / n.
* A naive analysis that pretends every shot has p = 0.7 would use sqrt(0.7 × 0.3 / n) instead.

The skewness and kurtosis of a sum of independent values can also be added up (through the third and fourth
cumulants), which gives exact formulas for the shooting percentage at every n. These are in `basketballPrediction()`
in functions.R.

```{r}
#| label: theory
theoryN <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 100, 200)
theory <- data.frame(
  n = theoryN,
  meanP = sapply(theoryN, function(n) mean(shotProbs(n))),
  exactSE = sapply(theoryN, basketballSE),
  naiveSE = sqrt(0.21 / theoryN),
  ratio = sapply(theoryN, basketballSE) / sqrt(0.21 / theoryN),
  skew = sapply(theoryN, function(n) basketballPrediction(n)["skew"]),
  exKurt = sapply(theoryN, function(n) basketballPrediction(n)["kurt"])
)
knitr::kable(theory, digits = 4, row.names = FALSE)
```

The exact SE is a little smaller than the naive one, about `r round(100 * (1 - theory$ratio[theory$n == 200]), 1)` percent for large n. The reason is that p (1 − p) is largest
at p = 0.5 and smaller for p away from 0.5, so shots with p = 0.9 or 0.8 vary less than a p = 0.7 shot. The skewness
is negative, because most shots have p above 0.5, so a low shooting percentage is the long tail.

# 2. What did you expect before running the simulation?

## Does the CLT still apply?

I expected the CLT to keep working even though every shot has a different p. The shots are independent, and the
Lindeberg version of the CLT, for independent values that are not identically distributed, holds when the sum of the
variances grows without bound and no single value dominates. Here every shot has variance p_t (1 − p_t) of at least
0.9 × 0.1 = 0.09, so the sum of the variances keeps growing with n, and every shot is only 0 or 1, so no single shot
can dominate.

## Center and spread

From the theory in section 1, I expected the mean of the shooting percentages to be 0.7 and their SD to follow the
exact SE sqrt(Σ p_t (1 − p_t)) / n at every n. This exact SE is about `r round(100 * (1 - theory$ratio[theory$n == 200]), 1)` percent smaller than the naive SE that uses
p = 0.7 for every shot. So the changing probabilities should shave a little off the variance, and the shooting
percentages should gather slightly more tightly around 0.7 than for a constant p.

## The n at which each check should pass

```{r}
#| label: prediction
nSearch <- 2:2000
predSkewAll <- sapply(nSearch, function(n) basketballPrediction(n)["skew"])
predKurtAll <- sapply(nSearch, function(n) basketballPrediction(n)["kurt"])
stepInSE <- sapply(nSearch, function(n) (1 / n) / basketballSE(n))
dieStep <- 1 / (populations$die$sigma * sqrt(8))
skewN <- min(nSearch[abs(predSkewAll) <= criteria$skew])
kurtN <- min(nSearch[abs(predKurtAll) <= criteria$kurt])
gapN <- min(nSearch[stepInSE <= dieStep])
c(skewN = skewN, kurtN = kurtN, gapN = gapN)
```

* Skewness: the exact formula reaches my cutoff of `r criteria$skew` at n = `r skewN`.
* Kurtosis: it is within `r criteria$kurt` from n = `r kurtN`.
* Gaps: the shooting percentage can only take the values 0, 1 / n, 2 / n, …, 1. As in 02die.qmd and 04binomial.qmd, I
  measured the step 1 / n in standard errors. It falls below the `r round(dieStep, 3)` SE at which the die passed at n = `r gapN`.

So I predicted that the gaps would be the bottleneck and decide the answer, at about n = `r gapN`. In 04binomial.qmd the
probability 0.1 was far from 0.5, so both the skewness and the gaps were problems. Here the average p of 0.7 is
closer to 0.5, so the skewness is solved quickly, at n = `r skewN`, and only the gaps remain.

## Does the fatigue matter?

I expected the overall shape to be very similar to a player who shoots with p = 0.7 on every shot
(Binomial(n, 0.7) / n), with only the small difference in the SE described above.

## One game of 20 shots

I expected the shooting percentage of a single 20 shot game not to be normal under my standard. Its predicted skewness
is `r round(basketballPrediction(20)["skew"], 3)`, which passes my cutoff, but the step between possible values is `r round((1 / 20) / basketballSE(20), 3)` SE, much larger than the
`r round(dieStep, 3)` SE at which the die passed. So the QQ plot should show clear steps.

# 3. Which sample sizes did you investigate?

## Coarse grid, then a finer grid

I started at n = 2, because with one shot the probability is just 0.9 and the "fatigue" does not exist. The coarse grid
covers my prediction of about n = `r gapN` with room on both sides.

```{r}
#| label: simulate
coarse <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200, 300, 500)
res <- searchN(basketballGenerator, coarse, mu = 0.7, theoSE = basketballSE, pred = basketballPrediction)
tab <- res$table
nStar <- smallestN(tab)
added <- setdiff(tab$n, coarse)
showTable(tab)
```

Here theoSE is the exact SE and predSkew, predKurt are the exact values. The finer grid added `r paste(added, collapse = ", ")`.

```{r}
#| label: whichFailed
failTable <- data.frame(
  n = tab$n,
  skewOK = abs(tab$skew) <= criteria$skew,
  kurtOK = abs(tab$exKurt) <= criteria$kurt,
  qqOK = tab$qqCor >= criteria$qqCor
)
knitr::kable(failTable)
skewPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(qqCor = 0, kurt = Inf)))
qqPass <- smallestN(tab, modifyList(criteria, list(skew = Inf, kurt = Inf)))
```

On its own, the skewness check passed from n = `r skewPass` (prediction `r skewN`) and the QQ check from n = `r qqPass` (prediction from the gaps `r gapN`).

## Fatigue against a constant p = 0.7

To see whether the changing p matters, I ran the same search for a player with p = 0.7 on every shot.

```{r}
#| label: constantP
constGen <- function(n) rbinom(n, size = 1, prob = 0.7)
constRes <- searchN(constGen, coarse, mu = 0.7, theoSE = iidSE(sqrt(0.21)),
                    pred = iidPrediction(-0.4 / sqrt(0.21), (1 - 6 * 0.21) / 0.21))
constTab <- constRes$table
constN <- smallestN(constTab)
compareN <- c(20, 50, 100, 200)
fatigueVsConstant <- data.frame(
  n = compareN,
  qqFatigue = tab$qqCor[match(compareN, tab$n)],
  qqConstant = constTab$qqCor[match(compareN, constTab$n)],
  sdFatigue = tab$simSD[match(compareN, tab$n)],
  sdConstant = constTab$simSD[match(compareN, constTab$n)]
)
knitr::kable(fatigueVsConstant, digits = 4)
```

The constant p = 0.7 player became normal at n = `r constN`, against n = `r nStar` with fatigue. The QQ correlations are almost the same
at every n, and the SD with fatigue is slightly smaller, as the exact SE predicted.

# 4. When did the sampling distribution become approximately normal?

$$\boxed{n = `r nStar`}$$

```{r}
#| label: summaryNumbers
star     <- tab[tab$n == nStar, ]
lastFail <- tab[tab$n == max(tab$n[tab$n < nStar & !tab$normalEnough]), ]
failed   <- c(skewness = abs(lastFail$skew) > criteria$skew,
              kurtosis = abs(lastFail$exKurt) > criteria$kurt,
              QQ = lastFail$qqCor < criteria$qqCor)
at20     <- tab[tab$n == 20, ]
at30     <- tab[tab$n == 30, ]
seRange  <- range(tab$seRatio)
naiveRatio <- tab$simSD / sqrt(0.21 / tab$n)
meanGapZ <- abs(tab$simMean - tab$theoMean) / (tab$theoSE / sqrt(num))
naiveOK <- abs(naiveRatio - 1) <= seTol
naivePassFrom <- min(tab$n[sapply(seq_along(naiveOK), function(i) all(naiveOK[i:length(naiveOK)]))])
```

My prediction from the gaps was n = `r gapN` and the simulation gave n = `r nStar`.

```{r}
#| label: whyN
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4.8
old <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
plot(tab$n, tab$qqCor, log = "x", type = "o", pch = 16, lwd = 2, ylim = c(0.97, 1),
     xlab = "Number of shots n (log scale)", ylab = "QQ correlation", main = "The gaps decide")
lines(constTab$n, constTab$qqCor, type = "o", pch = 1, lwd = 2, col = "darkorange", lty = 2)
abline(h = criteria$qqCor, col = "firebrick", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
abline(v = c(gapN, nStar), col = c("gray40", "steelblue"), lty = 3, lwd = 2)
legend("bottomright", c("Fatigue (0.9 to 0.5)", "Constant p = 0.7", paste("Cutoff", criteria$qqCor),
                        paste("Gap prediction n =", gapN), paste("Chosen n =", nStar)),
       col = c("black", "darkorange", "firebrick", "gray40", "steelblue"),
       lty = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 3), pch = c(16, 1, NA, NA, NA), lwd = 2, bty = "n", cex = 0.8)

plot(tab$n, tab$seRatio, log = "x", pch = 16, ylim = c(0.9, 1.1),
     xlab = "Number of shots n (log scale)", ylab = "Simulated SD / SE", main = "Exact SE against naive SE")
points(tab$n, naiveRatio, pch = 4, col = "darkorange", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 1, col = "gray40")
abline(h = theory$ratio[theory$n == 200], col = "darkorange", lty = 2)
legend("topright", c("Simulated SD / exact SE", "Simulated SD / naive SE (p = 0.7)"),
       col = c("black", "darkorange"), pch = c(16, 4), lwd = c(NA, 2), bty = "n", cex = 0.8)
par(old)
```

Left: with and without fatigue the QQ correlation follows almost the same path and crosses my cutoff near the gap
prediction. Right: the simulated SD matches the exact SE (black, near 1) and is consistently below the naive SE
(orange, near `r round(theory$ratio[theory$n == 200], 3)`).

# 5. How do the simulated mean and standard error compare with theory?

```{r}
#| label: seCheck
tab[, c("n", "simMean", "theoMean", "simSD", "theoSE", "seRatio", "seOK")]
```

Center: the simulated mean was within 2 Monte Carlo standard errors of 0.7 at `r sum(meanGapZ <= 2)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes (largest gap
`r round(max(meanGapZ), 2)`).

Spread: against the exact SE the ratio stayed between `r round(seRange[1], 3)` and `r round(seRange[2], 3)`, and `r sum(tab$seOK)` of `r nrow(tab)` sample sizes passed my 5 percent check.
Against the naive p = 0.7 SE the ratio was between `r round(min(naiveRatio), 3)` and `r round(max(naiveRatio), 3)`. The naive SE is not far off: it passes my 5 percent check
from n = `r naivePassFrom` on. But it is too large at every n, as predicted.

# 6. Why did you choose that value?

As for the die and the binomial, the histogram breaks are halfway between the possible values (1 / n apart). The red
curve is the normal curve with mean 0.7 and the exact SE.

```{r}
#| label: samplingPlots
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 6
plotLattice(res, nShow = unique(c(5, 20, nStar, 300)), mu = 0.7, theoSE = basketballSE, label = "Shooting percentage")
```

At n = 5 there are only six possible values and the QQ plot is a staircase. At n = 20, one game in the handout, the
histogram is roughly bell shaped but the steps are still large. At n = `r nStar` the steps are small and the QQ plot is
close to the line. At n = 300 the steps are hard to see.

```{r}
#| label: convergence
#| fig.width: 11
#| fig.height: 4
plotConvergence(tab, label = "Fatigue")
```

The skewness follows the exact prediction (red), and the kurtosis is small at every n.

Is one game of 20 shots enough? At n = 20 the skewness was `r round(at20$skew, 3)`, within my cutoff, but the QQ correlation was
`r round(at20$qqCor, 4)`, below `r criteria$qqCor`. So the shooting percentage of a single 20 shot game is not normal under my standard. At n = 30 the
QQ correlation was `r round(at30$qqCor, 4)`, also not enough.

I chose n = `r nStar` because:

* At n = `r nStar` the skewness was `r round(star$skew, 3)`, the excess kurtosis `r round(star$exKurt, 3)` and the QQ correlation `r round(star$qqCor, 4)`, all within my
  cutoffs, and every larger n I tested also passed.
* At the largest n that still failed (n = `r lastFail$n`), the check that failed was `r paste(names(failed)[failed], collapse = " and ")` (QQ correlation
  `r round(lastFail$qqCor, 4)`).
* The constant p = 0.7 comparison gave a similar n (`r constN`), so the answer comes from the gaps, not from the fatigue.

# 7. What surprised you?

```{r}
#| label: predictionCheck
predictionCheck <- data.frame(
  Prediction = c(
    "Mean 0.7 (about 95 percent of n within 2 Monte Carlo SEs)",
    "Exact SE holds; naive SE a few percent too large",
    paste("Skewness check passes at about n =", skewN),
    paste("Gaps decide at about n =", gapN),
    "Fatigue behaves almost like constant p = 0.7",
    "One game of 20 shots is not normal"
  ),
  Result = c(
    paste0("Within 2 Monte Carlo SEs at ", sum(meanGapZ <= 2), " of ", nrow(tab), " n"),
    paste0("Exact ratio ", round(seRange[1], 3), " to ", round(seRange[2], 3), "; naive ratio ",
           round(min(naiveRatio), 3), " to ", round(max(naiveRatio), 3)),
    paste("Skewness passed from n =", skewPass),
    paste("Answer n =", nStar),
    paste0("Constant p: n = ", constN, "; fatigue: n = ", nStar),
    paste("QQ correlation at n = 20:", round(at20$qqCor, 4))
  ),
  Match = c(ifelse(mean(meanGapZ <= 2) >= 0.9, "Same", "Different"), "Same", "Same", "Same", "Same", "Same")
)
knitr::kable(predictionCheck)
```

The broken assumption mattered as little as I expected, and seeing it was still striking. The shots are not
identically distributed, yet the shooting percentage became normal at almost the same n as for a player with a
constant p = 0.7, and the exact mean and SE formulas worked at every n. The general CLT for independent but not identical values (the Lindeberg CLT) only
needs that no single shot dominates the total, which is true here because every shot is 0 or 1.

The second surprise was that the step size rule from the die predicted the answer again (n = `r gapN` predicted, n = `r nStar`
found). The skewness here is small (`r round(basketballPrediction(100)["skew"], 3)` at n = 100), so, like Binomial(5, 0.5) in my 04binomial experiment, only the
gaps mattered.

The third observation is practical. The naive SE that pretends p = 0.7 for every shot is only about
`r round(100 * (1 / theory$ratio[theory$n == 200] - 1), 1)` percent too large, so for this amount of fatigue it would be a reasonable shortcut, but it is wrong in a
predictable direction: changing probabilities always make the total less variable than a constant probability with
the same average.

## Limitations

* I spread the same fatigue (0.9 down to 0.5) over every n. A real game with more shots might have more fatigue,
  which would be a different model.
* The shots are assumed independent; real shots could depend on each other (for example, confidence after a make).
* My standard counts the gaps, so the answer mainly measures how many shots it takes for the steps of 1 / n to become
  small, not the fatigue itself.
* All rows come from one random stream (seed `r student_id`), so they are not independent of each other.
